annotations.keyFindings: On twelve wards, electronic compliance rose from 48 to 71 percent with real-time feedback against 50 to 54 percent with silent monitoring; directly observed compliance was 64 against 57 percent.
annotations.limitations: Primary outcome measured by the feedback system itself; observers knew allocation; twelve wards.

annotations.keyFindings: Dispenser events were about three times higher while a visible observer was present, and the effect did not fade over eight weeks.
annotations.limitations: Four wards; covert counts do not measure compliance directly.

annotations.keyFindings: Badge systems detected 53 to 91 percent of observed opportunities; most feedback studies used the system's own measure as the outcome and only two were randomised.
annotations.limitations: Heterogeneous systems and outcomes; no pooled effect.

annotations.keyFindings: Nurses accepted ward-level feedback, objected to individual data use, and described touching dispensers to stop the badge vibrating without cleaning their hands.
annotations.limitations: Two surgical wards; questionnaire returned by 61 of 94 nursing staff.

annotations.keyFindings: No clear change in MRSA acquisition or hospital-onset C. difficile after dashboards, with 3.1 events a month and wide intervals.
annotations.limitations: Single hospital; underpowered for infection outcomes.

annotations.keyFindings: Intracluster correlation for observed compliance ranged from 0.04 to 0.09 (median 0.06); baseline compliance explained much between-ward variation.
annotations.limitations: Six source studies, mostly on medical wards.

annotations.keyFindings: Float staff carried feedback to control wards, shrinking the between-arm difference by about a third; pairing wards that share staff was recommended.
annotations.limitations: One trial; float status recorded retrospectively.

annotations.keyFindings: Hand rub consumption correlated weakly with observed compliance (r 0.31) and rose with acuity and visitors.

claims.text: In a ward-randomised trial, electronic compliance rose from 48 to 71 percent with real-time feedback against 50 to 54 percent with silent monitoring.
claims.passage: electronic compliance rose from 48 to 71 percent on feedback wards and from 50 to 54 percent on control wards
claims.interpretation: Feedback may change behaviour enough to justify a local trial; the outcome was the system's own measure.

claims.text: Hand hygiene events were about three times more frequent while a visible observer was present.
claims.passage: Dispenser events per hour were about three times higher when an observer was present
claims.interpretation: Direct observation must be equally visible in both arms, and absolute compliance will be overstated.

claims.text: A review of electronic monitoring recommends an outcome measured independently of the feedback system.
claims.passage: We recommend an outcome measured independently of the feedback system in any comparative evaluation.
claims.interpretation: The badge figure cannot be the primary outcome.

claims.text: Intracluster correlation for directly observed compliance ranged from 0.04 to 0.09 with a median of 0.06.
claims.passage: the intracluster correlation ranged from 0.04 to 0.09, with a median of 0.06
claims.interpretation: Planning values for the sample size, with baseline adjustment.

claims.text: Float staff reduced the between-arm difference by about a third in a ward-level feedback trial.
claims.passage: the difference between arms was about a third smaller than among staff who worked on one ward only
claims.interpretation: Randomise pairs of wards that share staff and record float status.

claims.text: Nurses described touching a dispenser to stop the badge vibrating without cleaning their hands.
claims.passage: Several nurses described touching a dispenser near the door to stop the badge vibrating during busy periods, without cleaning their hands.
claims.interpretation: Gaming makes the system's figure unreliable on feedback wards.

synthesis: Eight retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. One ward-randomised trial reported a large rise in electronic compliance with real-time feedback (48 to 71 against 50 to 54 percent), measured by the feedback system itself, with a smaller difference in observed compliance. A review of 31 studies and a staff study show why the system's own figure is a weak outcome: detection is incomplete and staff can satisfy the badge without cleaning their hands. Visible observers roughly triple hand hygiene events. Planning values for clustering are available (median intracluster correlation 0.06), float staff carry feedback between wards, and infections are too rare to compare in one hospital. Hand rub consumption is a weak proxy.
gradeRationale: One randomised trial with a system-measured primary outcome and several observational and methods records; direction consistent for electronic compliance but serious risk of measurement bias and indirectness for real hand hygiene. Certainty that feedback improves actual hand hygiene is low.
summary: Eight retrieved records appraised; six source-derived claims recorded with passages; overall certainty low.
